short_summary: Luxury hotels, farm shops, and global tourist spots are implementing strict bans and time limits on photography to combat disruptive influencer behavior and protect guest privacy.

sources.name: The Guardian
sources.title: ‘No influencers’: the hotels, restaurants and beauty spots restricting photoshoots

paragraphs: Across the globe, a growing backlash against content creators is reshaping how popular destinations handle photography and filming. Venues that were once considered merely photogenic are increasingly drawing the line against visitors who turn public spaces and dining rooms into private production sets. According to reports, the five-star Hotel du Cap-Eden-Roc in Antibes on the Côte d'Azur has instituted a strict policy requiring prior permission for any photoshoots. Hotel management noted that this intervention became necessary after guests booked lunch tables only to bring multiple bags of clothing and jewelry, spending their reservation changing outfits for social media rather than eating.

Less glamorous locations are facing similar pressures. The Hollies, a farm shop in Cheshire, enacted a ban on photography and filming between 10am and 4pm after drawing immense crowds. Prominent London restaurateur Jeremy King publicly complained that influencers were overrunning his establishments, declaring that enough was enough. International measures have grown equally inventive; a shop on Nantucket went viral for a sign prohibiting influencers, the town of Pomfret in Vermont banned photography in front of autumn foliage, and officials in Fujikawaguchiko, Japan erected a large screen to block tourists from taking pictures of Mount Fuji from a convenience store.

Venues argue that unbridled photoshoots directly jeopardize the privacy and discretion that guests pay substantial amounts to enjoy. Sophie Volant, manager of the Hotel du Cap-Eden-Roc, explained that while visitors are welcome, patrons ultimately expect their temporary summer residence to remain private. Anna Fedou, chief marketing officer at the Beaumier hotel group, emphasized that hospitality groups run places of rest rather than photo studios, stating that it remains their responsibility to protect the unique atmosphere and sense of space that travelers come to experience.

Industry observers suggest these new restrictions reflect a broader cultural shift away from continuous documentation and toward authentic presence. Alex Goat, founder of youth culture agency Livity, compared these emerging bans to nightclubs placing stickers over phone cameras to ensure patrons focus on the music. This trend encourages a mindset focused on enjoying the immediate environment rather than broadcasting it to online audiences.

At the same time, experts point out misconceptions regarding the economics of content creation. Nicole Ocran, founder of the Creator Union, explained that the vast majority of influencers produce content for free in hopes of catching the attention of commercial brands. Scholars like Sophie Bishop have also noted that harsh criticisms directed at influencer culture frequently carry underlying elements of sexism and snobbery, given that the industry is heavily feminized and bound to promotional culture. Even so, many creators acknowledge that some individuals occasionally cross boundaries and behave insufferably in public. Ultimately, as billions of people continue to engage with social media daily, advocates like Ocran hope that these rules might encourage a healthier and more balanced public attitude toward digital consumption.

facts.fact: The five-star Hotel du Cap-Eden-Roc in Antibes now requires prior permission for photoshoots after guests booked lunch reservations only to change outfits repeatedly for social media content.
The Hollies farm shop in Cheshire banned photography and filming between 10am and 4pm following heavy influencer traffic.
London restaurateur Jeremy King expressed frustration with influencers overrunning his establishments.

International measures against disruptive content creation include a viral sign on Nantucket, a town ban in Pomfret, Vermont during autumn foliage, and a screen erected in Fujikawaguchiko, Japan to block Mount Fuji views.
Venues argue that extensive photoshoots compromise the privacy and discretion expected by high-end guests.
Anna Fedou of the Beaumier hotel group noted that hotels are businesses of hospitality rather than photo studios, though some luxury groups selectively work with creators.
Alex Goat of the agency Livity compared these restrictions to phone camera sticker policies at clubs, signaling a return to experiencing spaces rather than documenting them.

Nicole Ocran of the Creator Union stated that most influencers generate content freely to court brands, while scholars like Sophie Bishop point out gendered and cultural stereotypes surrounding influencer backlash.
